newsitem.title: USA: U.S. coffee drinkers swallow price hikes -- for now.
newsitem.headline: U.S. coffee drinkers swallow price hikes -- for now.

text.p: Coffee drinkers are getting a jolt from higher coffee prices on the supermarket shelf but industry analysts say the extra cost is not spurring many to give up their morning cup of java.
"Consumers are not yet complaining about the price of coffee," said Donald Schoenholt, president of Gilles Coffee, a Brooklyn, N.Y.-based roaster. "But I believe that's going to change."

In the past four months, coffee futures at the Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York -- usually a forerunner of things to come at retail stores -- have more than doubled, fueled by worries about low coffee stock levels and poor crop prospects in Central and South America.
Last week, coffee for May delivery on the exchange jumped to $2.80 a pound, the highest level in two decades.
The surge in the cost of raw, unroasted beans has forced large commercial roasters and trendy cafe owners alike to pass along higher costs to their customers.
Roasting giants like Folgers Coffee Co., Starbucks and Maxwell House Coffee Co. have raised prices of ground coffee as futures soared.

On Monday, Folgers raised the list price on its standard 13-ounce can of ground regular coffee by 30 cents to $3.36 -- its fourth hike in the retail price since February with a total increase of $1.10, or more than 48 percent.
A can of Folgers decaffeinated coffee now lists for $4.06.

"I haven't heard of any consumer boycott," said David Dallis, president of Queens, N.Y.-based roaster and retailer Dallis Brothers. "I think people are taking it in stride. An 80-cent increase translates to a 2 cent-per-cup increase, it's still very affordable."

But the last time roasters jacked up prices -- following two severe, tree-damaging frosts in top-producer Brazil in 1994 -- a National Coffee Association survey revealed that the portion of the U.S. population drinking coffee had slipped to 47 percent from 50 percent in the early 1990s, and 75 percent during its post World War II peak.
The association's winter survey earlier this year showed a recovery to 49 percent, with per capita coffee consumption steady since 1995 at 1.7 cups a day.
Roasters worry that if prices continue to rise demand for coffee could fall by up to 10 percent on a global basis.
Some industry sources point out the current price rise has been gradual, while the move in 1994 was a sudden spike, a factor that could make retail price hikes easier to swallow.
"In 1994, the price increases were within a couple of weeks of each other, this has been more gradual and is not going to be as shocking," Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes said.
Jitters over the fast approaching Brazilian frost season are likely to sustain current prices, but if any deep freeze hits the biggest producer, analysts say prices could skyrocket.

Additionally, some market participants say high-quality arabica beans -- the type American consumers prefer and European drinkers are fast developing a taste for -- will probably stay in short supply at least until the new coffee crop becomes available this fall.
Coffee's soaring price has even caused producers to fret about a possible erosion in demand.

This week in London, the Association of Coffee Producing Countries -- whose members account for about 75 percent of the world's output -- meet to discuss whether to suspend their export quotas to help cool the explosive price rally.
If prices continue to climb and higher futures prices filter down to the consumer, industry sources expect it will be just a matter of time before coffee drinkers revolt.
